sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe accurate documentation of medications, including the elements that make a medication list complete and correct.
- Explain how to report medication discrepancies and errors through proper channels, including incident and adverse-event reporting.
- Recognize the importance of proper escalation and of never altering records improperly.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

The medication list is like a complete inventory of every pill, liquid, patch, and supplement a person uses. You need the whole list, not just part of it, so everyone knows what is safe.

### Question 2

Writing down a medicine is like labeling a box so no one confuses it with another: you record exactly what it is, how much, how often, and how it is taken.

### Question 3

A generic name is the medicine's 'family name' that stays the same no matter which company makes it, while a pill's color and logo can change.

### Question 4

Medicines from the store shelf and herbal products are still medicines to your body. Mixing them with prescriptions can be like mixing two strong cleaners — sometimes they don't go together.

### Question 5

Copying an order is like copying a recipe exactly: you don't change the amounts or guess, because a small change could ruin the result.

### Question 6

If a note is too messy to read, you ask the person who wrote it what it says instead of making up an answer. Guessing is never safe with medicine.

### Question 7

If someone says they take 'a little white pill,' you ask more questions or check the bottle. You never fill in the blank with a guess, because that could be the wrong medicine.

### Question 8

The 'best possible' list is like doing a careful home inventory by checking every room and every drawer, not just looking at one shelf.

### Question 9

Correcting a mistake in a record is like crossing out a word in a notebook with one neat line so people can still see what was changed, then signing next to it.

### Question 10

You should never 'whiten out' or erase a mistake in a patient's record, because that hides what happened. You make the fix in a way people can still see.

### Question 11

A late entry is like writing 'I forgot to mention this earlier, but here it is now' with the time written down so everyone knows it came later.

### Question 12

Every note needs a 'who' and a 'when,' like signing and dating a letter so people know it came from you and when you wrote it.

### Question 13

A medication list is like a living grocery list that changes often; you check it every time you shop, not just once a year.

### Question 14

Writing down an allergy is like putting a big red warning sticker on a food container so nobody accidentally uses the wrong ingredient.

### Question 15

An incident report is like writing down what happened when a toy broke, not to blame anyone, but to figure out how to keep it from breaking again.

### Question 16

A near miss is like a ball thrown at a window that someone catches just in time — nothing broke, but you learn to be more careful next time.

### Question 17

When something looks wrong, you tell the person in charge right away, like telling a teacher immediately instead of waiting weeks.

### Question 18

Reporting an error is like describing an accident to a coach: say exactly what happened, step by step, without calling anyone names.

### Question 19

Reporting a mistake that didn't hurt anyone is like fixing a loose step on a staircase before anyone trips on it.

### Question 20

MedWatch is like a safety hotline run by the government where doctors and others report when a medicine causes a serious problem.

### Question 21

Escalating is like raising your hand to ask the teacher for help instead of quietly guessing on a hard question.

### Question 22

When you are not sure something is right, you ask the person who knows instead of guessing, because a wrong guess can be dangerous.

### Question 23

A medical record is like a diary of facts: you write down what really happened, not what someone wants to read.

### Question 24

Going through the bag of bottles is like checking every item against a packing list to find anything missing, extra, or different.

### Question 25

If the list on paper doesn't match what the person actually takes, you write down the difference and tell the doctor, rather than quietly changing the list yourself.

### Question 26

If two of the same kind of medicine show up, you tell the doctor and write down the phone call. You don't tell the patient to stop or erase anything yourself.

### Question 27

If someone says they take more than the paper says, you write down exactly what they told you and tell the doctor — you don't edit the paper or change their medicine.

### Question 28

Some shortcuts are so easy to confuse that the rule is to spell them out or ask. 'QD' and 'QOD' look alike but mean very different things.

### Question 29

An error is like someone giving you the wrong key by mistake; a reaction is like the right key still jamming the lock. Different problems, different fixes.

### Question 30

If a medicine seems to be causing a big problem, you tell the doctor right away, like pulling a fire alarm instead of waiting to see if the fire goes out.

### Question 31

MERP is like a suggestion box for medicine mistakes, where people can safely say what went wrong so everyone can learn from it.

### Question 32

Writing down something that didn't happen is like telling a lie in an official notebook, and you should never help with it or ignore it.

### Question 33

Signing someone else's name or writing for them is like forging a signature on a permission slip — it's not allowed, no matter the reason.

### Question 34

If you find an old mistake, you tell the boss how to fix it properly instead of quietly rewriting history.

### Question 35

Fixing a note in a computer chart is like adding a sticky note that says 'correction' instead of ripping out the old page, so everyone can see what changed.

### Question 36

Backdating is like writing today's date on homework you did yesterday — it makes the record say something that isn't true about when it happened.

### Question 37

Repeating the order back is like repeating a phone number before hanging up, to make sure you heard every digit correctly.

### Question 38

Listing the right pharmacy is like writing the correct mailing address on a package so it arrives at the right house.

### Question 39

Writing down why each medicine is taken is like labeling each tool with what it's for, so you can spot if two tools do the same job.

### Question 40

If a patient's record says 'no peanuts' and someone orders peanut butter, you speak up before it's served, instead of quietly removing the warning.

### Question 41

An allergy is like the body's alarm system overreacting to a substance, while a side effect is a known, expected thing the medicine does.

### Question 42

To get the right information, you bring in a professional translator instead of guessing or using a family member, so nothing important is lost.

### Question 43

If a patient says they stopped a medicine, you write down what they said and tell the doctor, instead of erasing the old note or arguing with them.

### Question 44

A refill is like reordering a prescription from the doctor: you write down the request and wait for the doctor's 'yes' before sending it out.

### Question 45

Some medicine names are like two people with nearly identical names — easy to mix up, so you double-check carefully before writing one down.

### Question 46

Checking two identifiers is like confirming both the name and the birthday on a package so it goes to the right person.

### Question 47

High-alert medicines are like powerful tools that must be handled with extra care because a small mistake can cause big harm.

### Question 48

Controlled medicines are tracked like valuable items in a locked safe, with a careful log of every single one.

### Question 49

Even a free sample is a real medicine, so you write it down just like any other, so the list stays complete.

### Question 50

Recording how someone really takes their medicine is like noting how a plant is actually watered, so you know why it's thriving or wilting.

### Question 51

If a patient admits they sometimes forget their medicine, you kindly write it down and tell the doctor, instead of scolding them or hiding it.

### Question 52

The assistant spots the problem and hands it to the doctor, who makes the final call — like a referee making the final ruling.

### Question 53

Objective reporting is like a referee describing exactly what happened without taking sides or guessing.

### Question 54

When the list doesn't match, you collect clues and ask the expert, instead of guessing the answer yourself.

### Question 55

Recording a vaccine is like labeling a container with exactly what's inside, where it came from, and when, so it can always be traced.

### Question 56

If a patient says they don't take something on the list, you write down what they said and flag it, instead of erasing it right away.

### Question 57

These checks are like a pre-flight checklist for pilots: you go through each item carefully so nothing is missed.

### Question 58

Noting where each fact came from is like citing your sources in a report, so people know how reliable the information is.

### Question 59

An addendum is like adding a 'P.S.' to a letter with the date on it, without scribbling over the original words.

### Question 60

A list from another doctor is like another person's notes about a project — you compare them with your own and point out anything that doesn't match.

### Question 61

When two lists disagree, you don't pick a winner by habit — you check the facts and tell the person in charge.

### Question 62

Reporting properly is like turning in an official form to the right office, not just whispering about it in the hallway.

### Question 63

If you write the wrong thing, you neatly cross it out and sign it, and tell the boss if needed — you never try to hide it.

### Question 64

When someone has lots of medicines, you make one complete list of all of them and give it to the doctor to review, instead of deciding on your own what to leave out.

### Question 65

Writing down who prescribed each medicine is like noting who wrote each note, so you know exactly who to ask when something is unclear.

### Question 66

A ball caught before it hits the window is a near miss; a ball that hits the window but doesn't break it is still a hit. Both teach a lesson.

### Question 67

You write down what you observed, like 'the patient hasn't taken this medicine,' without calling names — because there could be many reasons why.

### Question 68

Bleeding with a blood thinner is like a warning light on the dashboard — you tell the mechanic right away instead of waiting for the next tune-up.

### Question 69

Insulin is a medicine where a tiny mistake matters a lot, so any question about it goes straight to the doctor, right away.

### Question 70

Big problems go to the person in charge, while tiny fixes you can handle yourself — like telling the principal about a real injury but fixing your own pencil mark.

### Question 71

Even with a fancy computer, you still double-check the order, because computers can still pick the wrong button.

### Question 72

Fixing a spelling mistake is like erasing a stray pencil mark, but changing what a note means is like rewriting a contract — you do it openly with a dated addition.

### Question 73

A rash plus trouble breathing is like smoke plus flames — you call for help right away, you don't wait or try more of what caused it.

### Question 74

The assistant writes down what they see and hear, while the doctor decides what it means and what to do — like a court reporter versus the judge.

### Question 75

Writing 'units' instead of a short 'U' is like writing the whole word on a warning label so nobody misreads it and gives ten times too much.

### Question 76

The right response is like fixing the problem, telling everyone who needs to know, and filling out the paperwork — without hiding anything.

### Question 77

When two names look almost the same, you check the original label twice, like double-checking two near-identical street addresses before delivering a package.

### Question 78

If the main person in charge is out, you tell the backup person in charge right away instead of letting a problem sit.

### Question 79

The audit trail is like a security camera in a store that records who did what and when, so nothing can be changed secretly.

### Question 80

MedWatch is like a national 'report a serious problem' box for medicines, used when something important and unexpected happens.

### Question 81

A blame-free culture is like a classroom where students feel safe raising their hands about mistakes, so the whole class can learn.

### Question 82

New confusion and falls are like clues that one of the medicines might not agree with the patient, so you tell the doctor instead of guessing.

### Question 83

The assistant copies and reports, but never rewrites the doctor's instructions to what they think is right — that's not their job.
